optionalSupplies: A few pieces of their usual dry food
substitutes: No screen? Drape a blanket over a chair.
No bed? A folded duvet in a corner.
title: Base Camp
clue: Every great climb starts with a long stay at the bottom, and no one is in a hurry.
reveal: A bonus for the first days and weeks with a new dog, adopted or a puppy. Climbers spend weeks acclimating before they go up; your dog gets the same: a cozy camp, a home that opens one door at a time and no timetable.
objective: Give a new-to-home dog a safe base, open the home one room at a time at their pace, and celebrate whichever camp they choose to rest in.
instructions: Build Base Camp before the dog explores: a bed or blanket in a quiet corner, fresh water, and a low screen or a draped chair so they can retreat. Close doors to the other rooms and keep visitors, children and other pets out of the camp room for now.
Camp One is the room itself. Sit nearby, low and quiet, and be a landmark: read, hum or just sit. Make no calls or approaches. The dog may sleep, watch or wander as they like.

When the dog looks relaxed, open Camp Two: one more door, such as the next room or the yard door. Stand at the threshold and narrate in a whispered 'real-estate agent' voice ('lovely light, excellent baseboards').
Leave a small welcome pack just inside: a cloth that smells of home, or a few pieces from their usual ration. Then step back. The dog may enter, stand, sniff or leave; nothing is asked.
If your dog does not come, leave the door open, close the viewing and try it tomorrow, or never. Staying at base camp is a perfect result.
When your dog chooses to rest in a room beyond Camp One, say nothing and wait. Later, when they have moved away, put their blanket there as the Summit Blanket.
Close the day by returning to Base Camp, putting out water and sitting quietly nearby. Add the next camp only when they seem ready, or not at all.
twist: The expedition runs on the dog's pace and veto: no timetable, no required summit, and base camp is allowed to be the whole trip.
variations: Open House day: show only one room per session in the whispered-listing voice, with a few pieces of ration scattered in each room.
Small apartment: the camps are corners, so Camp Two is the next corner and the window.
Puppy: keep sessions very short, plan lots of rest, and ask your vet before any outdoor camps or other dogs.
Yard camp: only once the dog is relaxed indoors, and only on a leash in a fully secure yard.
completion: The dog has had a safe base and the chance to explore beyond it. It counts even if they stay at Base Camp; there is no summit required, and no new dog needs it all done in a week.
photoIdea: The empty camp or a quiet view of the dog at rest from a distance. Skip posed shots.
memoryPrompt: Which camp did your dog reach, and what was the first thing they did when they got there?
supplies: A cloth that smells of home
dietNotes: Only a few pieces from the dog's usual ration, or skip food and use scent cloths; check any diet restrictions with your vet or rescue.
safety: Never pull or coax a dog into a room; some dogs need much longer than a rough timetable suggests.
Keep doors, windows and gates secure in the first weeks, and update ID and microchip details.
Puppies: ask your vet before outdoor camps or other dogs.
